Rules: real_exam/TEACHING_STYLE_GUIDE.md R1-R35 (no 'which way is better' verdict) + NITZAN_RHYTHM_DELIVERY.md P1-P13. Calm preset on the question reading and plain calculations.
slides: Let's continue with new operations, and look at a few more question types.

slides.say: Another type: they don't give you the definition at all. They only say that diamond of five is thirty. Someone took five, used the diamond, and got thirty. That's all you know.

The operation could be many different things. Six x is one example, because six times five is thirty. Five x plus five is another, because twenty-five plus five is thirty. So a question like this asks which definition cannot be the operation.
at: Five x plus five is another

slides.say: Your move is to go through the choices and put five into each one. A choice that gives thirty could be the rule. The one that doesn't give thirty cannot be the rule. For example, x squared plus five gives twenty-five plus five, thirty, so it could be the rule. But four x plus eight gives twenty plus eight, twenty-eight, so it cannot.

slides: In the exam, the moment you find the one that doesn't fit, you mark it and move on. In some question videos we'll check the other choices too, just to learn.

slides.say: Back to the star: three times the first number, plus the square of the second. Two star four is six plus sixteen, twenty-two. Four star two is twelve plus four, sixteen. Swap the inputs, and you get a different answer. So don't assume a new operation behaves like plus, where the order doesn't matter. Before you calculate, check which number goes into which slot.
Questions may ask: is a star b always equal to b star a? To show that it's not always true, one example where it fails is enough, like two and four.
at: To show that it's not always true

slides.say: To show that it's always true, numbers are not enough, because they only check some cases. One way is to write the rule with letters. Remember, the heart adds the two numbers, and then multiplies by five. So b heart a is five times the bracket b plus a. And b plus a is the same as a plus b, so b heart a is always equal to a heart b. For the heart, the order never matters. In a multiple-choice question, ruling out the other three choices also works.
One warning for order questions: don't test with two equal numbers. Four star four equals four star four for every operation, so it can't show anything about the order.
at: don't test with two equal numbers

slides.say: And if an input is unknown? Write the definition, and it becomes an ordinary equation. For example, x star four is twenty-five. By the definition, x star four is three x plus four squared, which is three x plus sixteen. So three x plus sixteen is equal to twenty-five. We want x alone, so subtract sixteen from both sides, and three x is nine. Then divide nine by three, and x is three.

Let's check it. Three star four has to give twenty-five. Three times three is nine, and nine plus sixteen is twenty-five. That's exactly the given, so it works. One more: k heart two is thirty-five. By the definition, that's five times the bracket k plus two. Five times the bracket is thirty-five. So divide thirty-five by five, and k plus two is seven. Subtract two from seven, and k is five.
at: and k plus two is seven

slides.say: On the exam you can also work back from the answers: put each choice into the rule, and see which one gives the result.
Let's sum up. Read the definition, and put each input in its slot, in brackets.

Work out what's inside each operation, and then turn the operation into a number. Nested operations go from the inside out. With no definition, test the input in each choice. For order questions, one example can show it's not always true, and letters can show it's always true. Nothing complicated here, just follow the rule exactly. [pause] I'll see you in the next video.
